name: System Design
description: Scaling, caching, queues, consistency, capacity estimation and the interview framework that structures all of it.

modules.name: Scaling Foundations
modules.description: How systems grow, and where they break when they do.

cards.prompt: Vertical vs horizontal scaling
cards.answer: Vertical means a bigger machine; horizontal means more machines behind a load balancer.

left.title: Vertical (scale up)
points: Simple: one node, one source of truth
Still a single point of failure

right.title: Horizontal (scale out)
points: Distributed systems problems arrive with it

cards.explanation: Scale up first — it is astonishingly far. A single modern server handles tens of thousands of requests per second. Scale out when you need availability, not just throughput; that is usually the real driver.

cards.prompt: Where can you cache, and what are the invalidation strategies?
cards.answer: Browser, CDN, reverse proxy, application memory, distributed cache (Redis), and the database's own buffer pool. Strategies: TTL expiry, write-through, write-behind, cache-aside, and explicit invalidation on write.
cards.explanation: Cache-aside is the default: read cache, miss, read database, populate. Watch for the three classic failures — stampede (many misses at once; use a lock or single-flight), penetration (repeated misses for a non-existent key; cache the negative), and avalanche (many keys expiring together; jitter the TTLs).

cards.prompt: Image upload triggers a slow transcode. How do you keep the API fast?
cards.answer: Accept the upload, enqueue a job, return 202 with a status URL. Workers consume the queue and update status; the client polls or receives a webhook or push event.
cards.explanation: Queues buy you decoupling, load levelling and retries. They cost you eventual consistency and new failure modes: duplicate delivery (make consumers idempotent), poison messages (dead-letter queues), ordering (only per partition) and backlog growth (alert on queue age, not just depth).

cards.prompt: How do you do back-of-envelope capacity estimation in an interview?
cards.answer: Start from users and behaviour: DAU × actions per day ÷ 86,400 = average QPS; multiply by 2–10 for peak. Then storage: bytes per record × records per day × retention. Then bandwidth: QPS × payload size. State assumptions out loud and round aggressively.
cards.explanation: Useful anchors: 86,400 seconds in a day, 1 M requests/day ≈ 12 QPS, a modern server handles ~10k QPS of simple work, a disk seek is ~1 ms while a memory read is ~100 ns. The point is demonstrating the reasoning, not the arithmetic.

resources.title: Latency numbers every programmer should know

cards.prompt: What is a good structure for a system design interview?
cards.answer: Clarify requirements and scope → establish functional and non-functional requirements (scale, latency, consistency, availability) → capacity estimates → API sketch → data model → high-level diagram → deep dive on one or two components → discuss bottlenecks and trade-offs.
cards.explanation: The failure mode is jumping straight to boxes. Interviewers are grading how you handle ambiguity and trade-offs, so narrate the alternatives you rejected and why. There is no correct answer, only defended decisions.

modules.name: Distributed Systems
modules.description: Consistency, coordination, failure and the patterns that keep systems up.

cards.prompt: What are the fallacies of distributed computing?
cards.answer: The network is reliable; latency is zero; bandwidth is infinite; the network is secure; topology does not change; there is one administrator; transport cost is zero; the network is homogeneous.
cards.explanation: Every one of these shows up as a bug: a missing timeout, an N+1 across the network, a chatty protocol, an unencrypted internal hop. Assume each call can be slow, fail, or succeed without you hearing about it.

cards.prompt: What problem do Raft and Paxos solve, and where do you meet them?
cards.answer: Getting a cluster to agree on a value (or a log order) despite crashes and network delays, with a majority quorum. You meet them inside etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul, Kafka's controller and most distributed databases.
cards.explanation: Quorum is why cluster sizes are odd: 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2. Consensus costs a round trip to a majority, so it is used for metadata and leadership, not for every data write. FLP says you cannot have consensus with guaranteed termination in a fully asynchronous system — hence timeouts and randomised elections.

cards.prompt: A downstream dependency slows to 30 s per call and your service falls over. What patterns prevent that?
cards.answer: Timeouts (always), a circuit breaker that trips after repeated failures and fails fast, a bulkhead limiting concurrent calls to that dependency, and a graceful degradation path.
cards.explanation: Without a bulkhead, one slow dependency consumes every thread or connection and takes down endpoints that never touch it. The breaker's half-open state probes recovery without flooding a healing service. Load shedding under overload beats queueing requests nobody is still waiting for.

cards.prompt: What problem does consistent hashing solve?
cards.answer: With `hash(key) % N`, changing N remaps almost every key. Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring so adding or removing a node moves only ~1/N of the keys.
cards.explanation: Virtual nodes even out the distribution and reduce hotspots when a node leaves. It underpins cache clusters, Cassandra, DynamoDB partitioning and CDN request routing — anywhere membership changes while traffic continues.

cards.prompt: An order spans payment, inventory and shipping services. There is no distributed transaction. How do you keep it consistent?
cards.answer: A saga: a sequence of local transactions where each step publishes an event, and every step has a compensating action to undo it if a later step fails. Choreography (events) for simple flows, orchestration (a coordinator) for complex ones.
cards.explanation: Two-phase commit across services couples availability to the slowest participant, so sagas trade atomicity for availability. You get intermediate states users can observe — 'payment taken, order pending' — which must be designed for, not hidden.

cards.prompt: Why is exactly-once delivery impossible, and what do you build instead?
cards.answer: A sender can never distinguish 'message lost' from 'acknowledgement lost', so it must retry — giving at-least-once. You build exactly-once *processing* on top: idempotent consumers plus deduplication by message id.
cards.explanation: Store the processed id in the same transaction as the effect; a repeat then becomes a no-op. Systems advertising exactly-once (Kafka transactions) provide it within their own boundary — the moment you call an external API, you are back to at-least-once.

modules.name: Building Blocks
modules.description: Log-based messaging, event-driven architecture, CQRS and event sourcing, ID generation, leader election, batch versus stream, and backpressure.

cards.prompt: How does a log-based broker such as Kafka differ from a traditional queue?
cards.answer: Messages are appended to partitioned, replicated logs and retained for a configured time rather than deleted when read. Consumers track their own offsets, so many independent consumer groups can read the same stream, and any of them can replay history. Within a consumer group, each partition goes to one consumer.
cards.explanation: Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, so choose the partition key for the ordering you need (all events of one order together). Partition count caps a group's parallelism. Replay makes logs ideal for event sourcing, CDC pipelines and rebuilding read models.

cards.prompt: Event notification vs event-carried state transfer
cards.answer: An event notification says something happened ("OrderPlaced id=42") and consumers call back for details; event-carried state transfer includes the data consumers need, so they can keep their own copy and never call back.

left.title: Event notification
points: Thin: an ID and a type
Consumers query the source for details
Source stays the single owner of data

right.title: Event-carried state transfer
points: Consumers work even when the source is down

cards.explanation: Event-driven systems decouple in time and ownership but make flows harder to see — invest in tracing and a catalogue of events. Treat event schemas as public contracts with versioning, exactly like APIs.

resources.title: Martin Fowler — What do you mean by "Event-Driven"?

cards.prompt: What are CQRS and event sourcing, and should they be used together?
cards.answer: CQRS separates the write model (commands enforcing invariants) from read models optimised for queries, often updated asynchronously. Event sourcing stores the sequence of domain events as the source of truth and derives current state by replaying them.
cards.explanation: They pair naturally — events feed the read models — but each is a large complexity cost: eventual consistency in reads, event schema evolution forever, and replay tooling. Use them where an audit trail, temporal queries or very different read and write shapes justify it, not as a default architecture.

cards.prompt: Auto-increment IDs vs UUIDv4 vs time-ordered IDs (UUIDv7, Snowflake)
cards.answer: Auto-increment is compact and ordered but needs one central sequence and leaks counts; UUIDv4 is random, generated anywhere without coordination, but scatters B-tree inserts; UUIDv7 and Snowflake-style IDs are generated anywhere and roughly time-ordered, keeping index inserts local.

right.title: UUIDv7 / Snowflake
points: Embeds a timestamp — mild information leak

cards.explanation: Time-ordered IDs are the modern default for distributed systems: no coordination, good index locality, and sortable by creation time. Never expose sequential IDs where enumeration matters (they reveal volume and invite IDOR probing) — and never rely on unguessable IDs as access control.

cards.prompt: How do you ensure only one instance runs a scheduled job or acts as leader?
cards.answer: Use a lease from a strongly consistent coordinator — etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul, a Kubernetes Lease object, or a database row with an expiry — renewed while the leader is healthy. If the leader stops renewing, another instance acquires the lease.
cards.explanation: A paused leader (GC pause, network partition) may still believe it leads after its lease expired, so two leaders can act at once. Fencing tokens — a monotonically increasing number checked by the resource being written — reject the stale leader's writes.

resources.title: Martin Kleppmann — How to do distributed locking

cards.prompt: Batch processing vs stream processing
cards.answer: Batch processes a bounded dataset at intervals (nightly jobs, Spark, SQL over a warehouse); streaming processes unbounded events continuously as they arrive (Flink, Kafka Streams), producing results with seconds of latency.

left.title: Batch
points: Easy to rerun on corrected data

cards.explanation: Batch is simpler, easier to reprocess and fine when hours of latency are acceptable. Streaming handles fraud detection, live dashboards and alerts, but brings windowing, late-arriving events and exactly-once-processing complexity. Many systems combine them.

cards.prompt: A downstream service can handle 1,000 requests per second, and upstream traffic spikes to 5,000. What should the system do?
cards.answer: Apply backpressure and load shedding rather than queueing without limit: bounded queues and concurrency limits, fast rejection (429/503 with `Retry-After`) of excess or low-priority work, and clients that back off. Queue only what can be processed within an acceptable latency.
cards.explanation: Unbounded queues turn overload into huge latency and memory exhaustion — requests are processed long after users gave up. Adaptive concurrency limits and prioritising critical traffic keep the system useful under load instead of uniformly failing.

resources.title: AWS Builders' Library — Using load shedding to avoid overload

modules.name: Design Walkthroughs
modules.description: Worked designs: URL shortener, rate limiter, news feed, chat, notification and file storage systems.

cards.prompt: Design a URL shortener. What are the key decisions?
cards.answer: Generate short codes by base62-encoding a unique ID (from a sequence, or a pre-allocated range per server) or by hashing with collision checks; store code → URL in a key-value store; serve redirects (302 if you need click analytics, 301 to let browsers cache) with a heavy cache in front, since reads vastly outnumber writes.
cards.explanation: Extras interviewers probe: custom aliases (uniqueness checks), expiry, abuse prevention (malicious URL scanning, rate limits), and analytics recorded asynchronously so redirects stay fast. Seven base62 characters give about 3.5 trillion codes.

resources.title: System Design Primer — Design Pastebin / URL shortener

cards.prompt: Design a distributed rate limiter for an API gateway handling 100k requests per second.
cards.answer: Keep per-key counters (user, API key, IP) in a fast shared store such as Redis using a token bucket or sliding-window counter updated atomically (Lua scripts), evaluated in the gateway. Return 429 with `Retry-After` and rate-limit headers.
cards.explanation: Trade-offs: a central store adds latency and a failure point, so decide whether to fail open or closed when it is unavailable. Local in-memory limits with periodic synchronisation scale further but are approximate. Sliding-window counters avoid the burst-at-boundary problem of fixed windows.

resources.title: Cloudflare blog — How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains

cards.prompt: Design a social news feed. Fan-out on write or fan-out on read?
cards.answer: Fan-out on write pushes each new post into every follower's precomputed feed (fast reads, expensive writes); fan-out on read assembles the feed from followed accounts at request time (cheap writes, slow reads). Real systems use a hybrid: push for normal accounts, pull for celebrities with millions of followers.
cards.explanation: A celebrity post fanned out on write would mean millions of writes at once — the "hot key" case. Feeds are stored as lists of post IDs in a cache, with post contents fetched and ranked separately.

resources.title: System Design Primer — Design the Twitter timeline and search

cards.prompt: Design a one-to-one and group chat service. What are the core components?
cards.answer: Persistent WebSocket connections to stateless chat servers, a presence/routing service mapping users to the server holding their connection, a message store partitioned by conversation (ordered by a per-conversation sequence), a queue for delivery to offline users with push notifications, and acknowledgements for delivered and read receipts.
cards.explanation: Ordering per conversation, idempotent delivery with client message IDs (to survive retries), and efficient history sync after reconnecting are the subtle parts. End-to-end encryption changes what the server can do — it can route but not read or search.

resources.title: System Design Primer — Design a chat system (exercises index)

cards.prompt: Design a notification system that sends email, SMS and push notifications for many products.
cards.answer: Producers publish notification requests to a queue; a service applies user preferences, rate limits and deduplication, renders templates, and routes to per-channel workers that call providers (email, SMS, APNs/FCM) with retries, backoff and dead-letter queues. Record delivery status and support idempotency keys.
cards.explanation: The hard parts are not sending: respecting opt-outs and quiet hours, avoiding duplicate or storm notifications during incidents, provider failover, and tracking delivery for support. Separate channels so an SMS provider outage does not delay email.

resources.title: Uber engineering — Uber's real-time push platform

cards.prompt: Design a file-sharing service like Dropbox. How do uploads and sync work?
cards.answer: Clients upload directly to object storage using presigned URLs (bypassing app servers), splitting large files into chunks identified by content hash for resumable uploads and deduplication. A metadata database tracks files, versions, chunks and sharing; a notification channel tells other devices to sync the changed chunks.
cards.explanation: Chunking with content hashes means editing one part of a large file re-uploads only the changed chunks, and identical content is stored once. Conflicts from offline edits are resolved by keeping both versions rather than guessing.

resources.title: System Design Primer — Object storage and CDN notes
